transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Daniel Park (Redwood AE), Meera Shah (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Novus Infra), Priya Nair (Novus SRE), Marcus Li (Novus CTO)

Summary:
High-level technical deep dive on multi-region routing and failover design for Novus' Redwood Private deployment. Covering policy-based routing, regional capacity constraints, indicators for automated failover, KV-cache replication/consistency strategies, cache warming and eviction, batching/throughput tradeoffs during failover, quantized model variant fallback, and DR tabletop/playbook suggestions.

Topics discussed:
- Policy routing: latency vs cost vs locality vs data residency
- Active-active vs active-passive region modes
- Health checks, circuit breakers, and canary funnels for routing decisions
- KV cache state: local caches, replication and cache-warm strategies, cold-start mitigation
- Batching and throughput: how continuous batching behaves during traffic shifts / spike scenarios
- Quantization variant fallbacks: accuracy vs perf regressions and how to route to them selectively
- Private/VPC considerations: egress rules, inter-region network topology, and security for cross-region replication

Transcript body:
00:00 Daniel (AE): All right um hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro from our side Meera will run the deep dive and I'll field the non-technical bits. Could you quickly say where you're at with regions?
00:12 Lina (Novus): Sure yeah uh we have prod in us-east-1 and eu-west-1, we"re starting to pilot ap-southeast-1 for latency-sensitive apps. Peak traffic today is ~2k TPS across east-us with spikes to 3k during morning windows.
00:29 Meera (SE): okay great, that helps. Our goal today is to walk through multi-region routing policies and failure modes—so how we decide to steer traffic, what health signals to use, and how to recover with warm caches and model fallbacks.
00:45 Priya (SRE): quick note, compliance requires that some PII queries stay in eu-west-1 only; we can't route that out.
00:53 Meera: yep we"ll cover routing rules that respect data residency and sticky routing for those routes.
01:05 Marcus (CTO): Also interested in RTO/RPO assumptions, what happens if an entire region loses access to the KV-store or the k-v cache becomes stale after failover.
01:16 Meera: excellent, so first high-level options: active-active with global traffic steering (low latency, needs cache replication or cache warming), versus active-passive with DNS/GW failover (simpler but slower RTO).
01:33 Daniel: to add, cost and infra complexity go up with active-active. You pay for replicated capacity but get better failover and lower latency.
01:42 Meera: let me sketch policy examples. (small pause) 01:51 Meera: Policy A: latency-first — route to nearest healthy region, fallback to next nearest. Health checks are per-route and per-model; we use token-level latency percentiles (p95) + error-rate. Policy B: capacity-aware — only route if target region has available reserved slots; otherwise fallback. Policy C: residency-first — force routing for sensitive data to region-bound endpoints only.
02:20 Lina: On that capacity-aware note, how do you detect available slots in Dedicated vs Private? We have reserved GPU pools but there are other internal jobs that might use them.
02:33 Meera: within Redwood Private we surface a capacity metric: available concurrent sessions and projected throughput based on model profile and quantization. For private deployments we can integrate with your scheduler to surface real-time capacity signals. In cases where the scheduler is ambiguous we recommend conservative thresholds to avoid overcommit.
02:52 Priya: okay and how about the KV cache, if we have local caches per-region how do we keep them consistent? We can't afford long RPOs for context caching for some chat flows.
03:05 Meera: good question. There are tradeoffs: synchronous cross-region replication gives stronger guarantees but high write latencies. We typically advise a hybrid: critical context stored in the primary region with async replicate and application-level reconciliation; for most workloads prefix/KV cache is best-effort and we treat cross-region as eventual. For chat state we recommend pinning sessions to a region for duration of conversation (session stickiness) to avoid cross-region fetches.
03:34 Daniel: we can also do selective replication: replicate small session-metadata for quick reconstructions (like last 3 turns) while full history remains single-region.
03:44 Marcus: so in a full-region outage what are the options for rehydrating caches in the failover region quickly?
03:52 Meera: strategies: 1) cache-warm using prioritized recent sessions — Redwood can export last-N sessions (if allowed) to the failover region and preload. 2) on-request lazy rebuild with a warmed KV promotion queue — requests hit cold cache for a short period but we prioritize their rebuild. 3) run a parallel replay from log stream to rebuild (depends on your audit/log retention). Each has tradeoffs in RTO and complexity.
04:25 Priya: is there an automated warmup tool in Redwood?
04:29 Meera: we have a cache-warm playbook; in Private deployments we can run an orchestrated warm-up job that replays recent prefixes into the KV store in target region. It requires cross-region transfer access and is something we run as part of DR.
04:43 Lina: networking wise if we do active-active, are you using anycast or DNS-level steering? We"re concerned about sticky sessions and TLS termination.
04:52 Meera: for hosted we use a mix: anycast + edge LB for low-latency routing. For private deployments customers usually prefer DNS + region-aware gateway to control egress and TLS termination inside VPC. We recommend edge termination only when compliance allows; otherwise terminate inside the VPC and use regional gateways with client-side routing logic or internal load balancing.
05:15 Daniel: note that DNS TTLs and propagation are factors; Route53 health checks with low TTLs still have windows. Traffic Director style control plane is better for sub-second steering if you have global LB.
05:29 Marcus: what's your health-check set? Is it purely ping/HTTP or do you do synthetic token-level passes to the model?
05:37 Meera: we do layered checks: infra-level (node up, GPU avail), service-level (inference endpoint returns 200), and synthetic inference checks — small synthetic prompts to verify latency and correctness. For routing decisions we weight synthetic p95 latency and error-rate more heavily than single request success.
06:00 Priya: and circuit breakers? If a region is degraded we want to rate-limit traffic before failing over, right?
06:07 Meera: yes we implement circuit-breakers with thresholds: e.g., if p95 latency > configured threshold OR error-rate > X% for 2 consecutive windows, start funneling small percents of traffic to fallbacks (canary), then increase until shifted. This avoids big cold-start thundering.
06:24 Lina: how do you handle batching when traffic shifts quickly? Batching decreases latency per token for throughput but initial requests may block waiting for batch.
06:34 Meera: Redwood runtime uses continuous batching; during surge we throttle batch windows to maintain latency SLOs — we can prioritize small interactive routes with lower batching windows while larger background jobs get larger batch sizes. During failover you can temporarily favor lower batch latencies to reduce tail for new region cold starts.
06:53 Daniel: also, if you have quantized model variants in other regions, you might decide to route a small percent of requests there — but be aware of small quality deltas. It's useful as an interim capacity fallback.
07:06 Marcus: curious, do you automatically fall back to quantized when you detect capacity pressure? Or is that manual?
07:13 Meera: it's configurable: Policy X can opt to fall back to quantized variants automatically when capacity or p95 exceeds thresholds. We tag routes with quality budgets so you can say route up to 10% of requests to lower-precision models for non-critical traffic.
07:29 Priya: security question: cross-region replication of context — how do you handle encryption and KMS?
07:35 Meera: Redwood Private integrates with customer KMS/HSM for keys; we encrypt data in transit and at rest. For cross-region replication we recommend separate CMKs per region or use a centralized KMS with strict IAM, depending on your compliance. We also provide audit logs for replication events.
07:54 Lina: timeline wise, what would you recommend for our plan? We need RTO < 30 mins for core chat, RPO <= 5 mins for session metadata.
08:02 Meera: pragmatic path: 1) active-passive with automation — automate DNS/GW failover, plus a cache-warm orchestration to reduce RTO to target. 2) medium-term: active-active for core low-latency routes with session stickiness and selective replication for last-3-turns; reserve capacity in secondary region.
08:22 Daniel: we'll put together a failover playbook with shell steps, and a DR tabletop checklist for your folks.
08:29 Meera: one more thing — observability: expose per-route token-level latency by region, cache-hit ratios, and replica lag. Those signals are key for deciding failover rather than pure infra checks.
08:43 Priya: can you show an example runbook step for a region outage?
08:48 Meera: sure quick example: 1) detect: synthetic p95 > threshold & node heartbeat missing; 2) mark region unhealthy in control-plane; 3) enable circuit-breaker and funnel 5% to fallback region; 4) run cache-warm job for top-1000 sessions; 5) if stable increase to 50%, then 100%; 6) post-recovery reconcile KV store and audit logs. We'll write this out with concrete commands for your infra.
09:20 Marcus: and the manual approvals? We want an option to make it manual for the first run.
09:25 Daniel: we can set the policy to manual escalation with a runbook step that requires a button press in Console.
09:31 Lina: small nit — are there any known failure modes with route flapping during unstable network?
09:36 Meera: yes route flapping can cause oscillation; mitigation: add hysteresis and backoff windows plus global leader-election to avoid split-brain. Also avoid overly aggressive TTLs.
09:50 Priya: last Q: for the bench you mentioned, what do you need from us?
09:54 Meera: sample traffic shape, top prompt sets, sample PII routes (tagged), and a test harness endpoint to run our runner against. We'll run latencies under failover scenarios and measure cold-cache RTO.
10:06 Daniel: OK we'll follow up with a doc and a diagram. Anything else?
10:10 Marcus: looks good, thanks everyone.

Recap (end):
- Redwood to provide routing diagram, failover runbook, and example circuit-breaker thresholds (Daniel).
